title: Role of basal ganglia and cerebellar inputs to motor thalamus in gait
text:
Walking is essential for everyday life, and gait disturbances are among the most disabling symptoms in a
range of neurological disorders, including Parkinson’s disease. This study proposes to determine the functional
role of the motor thalamus, a central motor hub, and its inputs from basal ganglia and cerebellum in the control
of gait, as well as its alterations in Parkinson’s disease mouse models. The results of this work will contribute
to our understanding of how the brain controls gait, and inform the development of better treatment
approaches for gait disturbances.

title: Cancer Bioinformatics: Data analysis and method development for the Yale Cancer Center
text:
OVERALL PROJECT NARRATIVE
Cancer is a genetic disease driven by somatic or inherited mutations and, thus, genomic
technologies, particularly next-generation sequencing and bioinformatic analysis, have made
significant impact on cancer diagnosis, management, and treatment. However, unlike
laboratory protocols and benchwork, researchers find it difficult to bring the necessary expertise
in bioinformatic data analysis into their labs. The support of this R50 award will allow Dr. Lopez-
Giraldez to provide broader bioinformatics analysis access and training to Yale Cancer Center
researchers, and to expedite the progress, enable innovative NGS technologies, and enrich the
scope of their research.

title: Structural and functional definition of human astrovirus-receptor interactions
text:
Astroviruses are a global cause of gastroenteritis, commonly known as stomach flu, but currently there are no
vaccines or treatments available to protect against these viruses. Identifying which human factors these viruses
subvert to infect the intestine is critical for the generation of much-needed tools to study astroviruses in cell
culture and in animal models. Defining these factors will also reveal key targets for novel antiviral therapies to
prevent infection.

title: Molecular mechanisms driving therapy-induced lineage plasticity
text:
Lineage plasticity is a developmental process of cell reprogramming employed by cancer cells as a mechanism
of therapy resistance. Dr. Linares’s application for the R50 Research Specialist Award will support Dr.
Diaz-Meco’s research program focused on elucidating the molecular mechanisms that regulate lineage plasticity
in prostate tumors. Unveiling the mechanisms that control this process is crucial to find new targets for
castration-resistant prostate cancer.

title: Unravelling the Role of Epigenetics and Cytokines in Type 2 Diabetes among African-ancestry Populations
text: African-ancestry populations in the US and Europe are disproportionately affected by type 2 diabetes (T2D), while rates are rapidly increasing in sub-Saharan Africa. The reasons for this disproportionate burden are poorly understood but are thought to be a complex interplay between genetic and environmental factors, such as lifestyle. Previous work led by the candidate demonstrated that T2D in Africans can partly be traced back to DNA methylation-an important epigenetic mechanism that is a key mediator in the interplay between genetics and lifestyle factors. It also suggested that variations in circulating cytokines, partly driven by African-ancestry specific genetic variants, may play a role in the biology of T2D in Africans. The mentored phase of the Pathway to Independence award enabled the candidate to acquire the necessary knowledge and skills to build on this work. An outstanding mentoring committee guided her in mastering causal inference methods, including the application of Mendelian randomization approaches to epigenetic data, polygenic prediction, and mediation analysis, as well as multi-omics analysis. The Center for Research on Genomics and Global Health (CRGG H) at the National Human Genome Research Institute (NHGRI), renowned for its genetics and genomics research in diverse populations, especially African-ancestry populations, provided an ideal environment for the candidate's training du ring the K99 phase of the project. By inferring causality in the previously observed associations between DNA methylation, circulating cytokines, and diabetes, the candidate was able to identify specific DNA methylation sites causally associated with T2D in Africans through two-sample Mendelian randomization approaches. The candidate also identified three circulating cytokines causally associated with insulin sensitivity and beta-cell function, the hallmarks of T2D pathophysiology. To further improve our understanding of the etiology of T2D in Africans, it is imperative to better understand what drives variation in the circulating cytokines causally associated with T2D in Africans. Given the complex interplay of genetic and environmental factors in T2D etiology, the candidate aims to identify both lifestyle and genetic factors causing variability in these cytokines. To achieve this, the candidate will leverage data from two existing cohorts: sub-Saharan Africans living in Africa from the AADM study and sub-Saharan Africans living in Africa and Europe from the RODAM study. To test the hypothesis that both lifestyle factors and genetic regulatory mechanisms drive variation in circulating cytokines relevant forT2D in Africans, the candidate will accomplish two specific aims. Aim 1 is to infer causality in lifestyle-cytokine associations using Mendelian randomization approaches. Aim 2 will identify regulatory mechanisms of cytokines using multi-omics data. Mechanisms by which loci identified in the candidate's published GWAS analyses exert their effect will be studied using genotype, whole genome sequence, DNA methylation, RNA-seq data, and metabolic data. The training received during the mentored phase significantly enhanced the candidate's skill set, allowing the candidate to develop into an independent investigator and lead a lab at the University of Maryland aimed at studying cardiometabolic diseases among African-ancestry populations.

title: Extracellular matrix-derived chemokines mediate smoking-associated coronary atherosclerosis
text:
Coronary artery disease (CAD) is a chronic inflammatory vascular condition that remains a
leading cause of death in the United States with disproportionate impact on the US veteran
population. Cigarette smoking and other tobacco products clearly accelerate the development of
CAD; however, the cellular and molecular mechanisms linking smoke with CAD remain poorly
understood. In this proposal, we present the matrikine proline-glycine-proline (PGP) and
exosome-associated proteases (i.e. proteolytic exosomes) as novel mediators of smoke-induced
atherosclerosis. We propose an integrative mouse model of smoke-induced atherosclerosis to
investigate the pathogenic role of PGP and its generating proteases. Our pre-clinical experiments
will be complimented by translational studies among veterans with CAD. Ultimately, PGP and
proteolytic exosomes may represent new biomarkers and targets for the prevention of CAD.

title: Role of CYB5R3 in erythropoiesis
text:
This study will elucidate the role of erythroid cell-specific cytochrome b5 reductase 3 (CYB5R3) in erythropoiesis.
The findings from this research have the potential to address a critical gap in our understanding of redox signaling
in erythrocyte biology and may contribute to the development of novel therapeutic strategies to alleviate the
significant global burden of anemia.

title: Regulatory networks in lens development
text:
Cataracts impact lens transparency and its surgery accounts for substantial costs to the US Medicare budget
(>$3.4 billion annually), as ~50% of Americans aged 80 and above are affected by cataract (and its prevalence
is expected to double by 2050, further straining the US Medicare budget). Thus, to prevent or delay cataract, it
is essential to define the mechanisms that contribute to the formation of the lens and to the maintenance of its
transparency. The proposed research will result in the characterization of new mechanisms and pathways in
lens development, homeostasis and pathology and will continue development of a publicly available web-
based interactive bioinformatics tool – for both clinicians and scientists – that facilitates prediction and
prioritization of genes/pathways to further accelerate cataract gene discovery.

title: Project 1 - Sweeney_Hammers
text: The multifaceted pathologies associated with muscular dystrophies, particularly Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), represent major challenges to the development and clinical implementation of effective therapeutics for these diseases. AAV gene therapies delivering micro-dystrophin transgenes to all striated muscles are now in the clinic, with hopes of bringing transformative outcomes course of DMD disease. However, much work is still needed to advance the safety and efficacy of these therapies before widespread implementation for the treatment of DMD. In the clinic, there have been serious and fatal responses to viral capsids and the expressed transgenes. Furthermore, we have found that certain micro-dystrophin designs can hasten onset of lethal cardiomyopathy in mice. The goal of the current project is to develop next-generation AAV gene therapies for DMD that a) avoid transgene safety concerns and b) reduce the immune response to vector delivery, thereby advancing the path to safe, effective, and broad-use AAV gene therapies for muscular dystrophies. In Aim 1, we will develop novel utrophin-dystrophin chimeric transgenes that are less immunogenic than their micro- dystrophin counterparts. Aim 2 seeks to improve the design AAV capsids and vector genomes to reduce risks of provoking severe immune responses during treatment. It is anticipated that progress towards these aims will significant advancements towards safe and efficacious implementation of gene therapy for DMD and other muscular dystrophies.

title: Long-read, single-cell RNA sequencing of high-risk neuroblastoma samples
text:
The majority of patients with high-risk neuroblastoma, the most common extracranial solid tumor of
childhood, die despite intensive cytotoxic therapies; and survivors are burdened with treatment-related co-
morbidities. While immunotherapy with dinutuximab can be very effective, it is also highly toxic, and relapses
still occur in at least half of patients. Upon completion of this next-generation RNA sequencing project, we will
be in the position to nominate additional non-canonical surface proteoforms as targets for adoptive T cell
immunotherapy.

title: The MusicGens Consortium: Growing robust and rigorous approaches to musicality genomics
text:
Public Health Narrative
This project brings together world experts in complex traits genetics and music cognition to
understand how DNA variation relates to many aspects of human musicality. By providing
support for the annual meeting of the Musicality Genomics Consortium, we provide an important
intellectual resource for this emerging field. Research findings may reveal new clinical-
translational applications that could emerge from new knowledge of how and why human
musicality unfolds over the lifespan.

title: Cell and Tissue Imaging Facility
text: Cell and Tissue Imaging Facility (CTIF) The goal of the Cell and Tissue Imaging Facility (CTIF) is to provide UPMC Hillman Cancer Center (HCC) members with a “cutting-edge” resource equipped to address all research-related microscopy needs and expert advice on experimental design and data analysis. The imaging specialties offered by CTIF include: light and fluorescence microscopy (macro-dissecting light and fluorescence, epi-fluorescence, confocal scanning, and multi-photon imaging); live cell microscopy (transmitted light and fluorescence) and fluorescence specialties including fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET), spectral analysis, ratiometric imaging, super-resolution microscopy (stimulated emission depletion microscopy [STED] structured illumination microscopy [SIM] and stochastic optical reconstruction microscopy [STORM]) technologies), light sheet approaches (both macro and lattice), ribbon scanning ultrafast confocal microscopy; ultrastructural electron microscopy (transmission electron microscopy [TEM], scanning electron microscopy [SEM], immuno-electron SEM and TEM. In addition, the faculty and staff of CTIF provide expertise for assisting with experimental design, instrument use, software use, and complex imaging and analysis methods. Furthermore we are expert in the development and application of computer aided morphometric analysis methods and actively develop algorithms for quantitation of events in living and fixed material.

title: Core B: MPN-RC Tissue Bank
text:
Core B Project Narrative
The Core B Tissue Bank is an essential resource of the Myeloproliferative Neoplasms-Research Consortium
(MPN-RC) which receives, processes and stores tissues collected from MPN patients consented under IRB
approved Protocol 106 (Project 4), as well as patients on Project 4 clinical trials. Core B provides a central
repository for these tissues that are associated with clinical and mutational annotation (Core C), which enables
appropriate selection of specimens for each project. Specimens are distributed to MPN-RC investigators and the
larger scientific community for translational research and clinical trial specimens are utilized for biomarker and
pharmacodynamic analysis of novel therapies (Core D).

title: Mechanistically Guided Immunometabolic CAR-TIL Therapy for Glioblastoma Heterogeneity and Immune Suppression
text:
Glioblastoma (GBM) is a highly aggressive primary brain tumor with poor prognosis due to cellular heterogeneity
and a profoundly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). This project develops dual-engineered
ME1-armored anti–PD-L1 CAR tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (CAR-TILs) combined with pharmacologic
metabolic sensitization (clemastine + bexarotene) to enhance tumor eradication. By evaluating the impact of
these intracranial therapies on the tumor, TME, and central nervous system (CNS) cell populations, including
neurons, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes, this research establishes a mechanistic framework for metabolically
guided immunotherapies, develop a future clinical trial, and advances strategies for improving outcomes in GBM
and other neuroinflammatory disorders.

title: Drug Selection and Direct Reprogramming in Generation and Culture of Otic Progenitors
text:
The stem cell like capabilities of otic progenitors giving rise to sensory hair cells and supporting cells may be key
in developing novel strategies for treating hearing loss. We propose to use inner ear stem cells and induced otic
progenitors to identify critical pathways, transcription factors, and gene regulatory networks that mediate the
stem cell potential of otic progenitors. Our findings would enhance understanding of otic progenitors during
development and could potentially lead to novel strategies for cell-based treatment of hearing loss.

title: Uncovering Patterns in the Evolving Drug Supply to Detect Emerging Overdose Trends Using Machine Learning
text:
This research addresses the U.S. drug overdose crisis by leveraging advanced machine learning techniques to
detect shifts in the illicit drug supply and assess their impact on fatal overdose trends. By integrating drug
seizure data from the National Forensic Laboratory Information System with county-level overdose mortality
data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, this study will identify county-level warning signals
of emerging high-risk substances and polysubstance combinations. These insights will inform policy decisions
and strengthen localized overdose prevention strategies to mitigate overdose-related harm.

title: Glutamate receptors and human neurological disease
text:
Glutamate-activated NMDA receptors mediate a Ca2+-permeable component of excitatory
synaptic transmission in the brain that is involved in learning, memory, and development.
NMDA receptors have been implicated in a wide range of neurological conditions, and there is
intense interest in the development of allosteric modulators as new therapeutic treatments for
neurological disease. This research program is designed to address all key aspects of glutamate
receptor signaling, including the structural underpinnings of function, genetic variation as it
relates to rare disease and risk factors, identification of therapeutically-relevant molecules that
can be used as probes to develop novel treatment strategies, and the fundamental process of
synaptic transmission.

title: Exploiting immunostimulatory microbial pattern recognition to improve head and neck cancer therapy
text:
Current management of head and neck cancer including radiation therapy or immunotherapy has not
significantly improved the overall survival of patients with advanced HNSCC. This application aims to test a
novel molecular platform with a built-in microbial sequence that can potentially achieve robust and long-lasting
antitumor immunity to enhance cure rates by overcoming the therapeutic barriers in the tumor
microenvironment.

title: Characteristics and Determinants of Post-COVID Neurocognitive Dysfunction
text:
Neurologic and mental health complications are among the most common post-acute sequelae of COVID-19
infection. A recent study showed that Veterans surviving COVID-19 had over 80% increased risk of mental
health diagnosis over the subsequent year. They might linger or worsen over time. Characteristics, predictors,
and mechanisms of these complications remain unclear. We are planning to leverage a well-characterized
cohort of Veterans with and without COVID-19 diagnosis to administer careful serial neuropsychological testing
over up to three years to better characterize these complications and to establish whether antiviral therapy is
preventive of cognitive impairment. We will also study blood biomarkers of brain damage and advanced
imaging on a subset of these patients to determine whether these predict and/or explain the neurocognitive
changes. A successful completion of these aims will establish benchmarks to analyze and manage neurologic
and mental health changes following acute COVID-19 infection.

title: Telomerase RNP Prisonbreaks from Phase-Separated Nuclear Body
text:
Phase separation is a common cell biology phenomenon with unsolved implications in human aging and
neurodegenerative diseases. Specialized instruments, such as the NanoLive microscope, can visualize phase-
separated cell structures in living cells for a long period at unprecedented resolution, without harming cells. The
use of it in our program will lead to new knowledge in phase separation biology and likely new drug targets to
treat aging-related symptoms.
